name: The Great Plane of Sydney Gardens

location.address: Beside the path just before the Kennet and Avon Canal bridge, Sydney Gardens, Bath

story:
This plane is thought to be older than the park it stands in. The Sydney Gardens tree trail dates its planting to 1777, eighteen years before Sydney Gardens was laid out in 1795, which would mean the garden's makers drew their paths around a tree that was already there. The trail says "thought to", and so do we. Nobody has counted its rings, and the date is the gardens' own best estimate, not a record.

The size is not an estimate. The tree stands 28 metres tall with a trunk 6.6 metres round, the largest of the gardens' planes, measured for the 2021 trail from an arboricultural survey made the year before for the restoration of the park.

If the 1777 date holds, this trunk has watched the whole history of the place happen a few metres from its roots. The ornate bridge just down the path carries the date 1800, when the Kennet and Avon Canal came through. From 1839 the Great Western Railway was cut through the gardens too, so a Georgian pleasure ground ended up with a canal and a main line running across it, and this plane outlasted the arrival of both.

Not every big plane makes it. A felled trunk on the lower lawn belonged to another of the gardens' planes, cut down in 2018 because of fungus. This one is still growing, labelled as stop 8 on the trail, on the way down to the canal.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, 6.6 metres round and 28 metres tall, the biggest plane in Sydney Gardens. It stands on the left of the path coming down from the great beech, just before the ornate canal bridge.

name: The Beech of Sydney Gardens

location.address: Beside the path near the Sydney Road entrance, Sydney Gardens, Bath

story:
This beech may have started life as part of a hedge. The Sydney Gardens tree trail suggests it was one of a line of beeches planted around the Ride when the gardens opened in 1795, and that it simply never stopped growing. The hedge plant, if that is what it was, now stands 30 metres tall with a trunk 4.5 metres round.

The hedge is an inference, and the trail is careful to present it as one. What it says with more confidence is that the tree is large enough to belong to the gardens' original planting, which would put it at something over 200 years old and, in the trail's words, among the oldest trees in the park. No planting record survives for it, so treat the date as a reading of its size rather than a fact on paper.

If the trail is right, the beech went in for a Georgian pleasure garden and has stood on the same spot ever since, through the arrival of the Kennet and Avon Canal around 1800 and the Great Western Railway cutting from 1839, both of which run through the same gardens a short walk away. Its neighbours today are rather less grand. It stands near the entrance off Sydney Road, above the tennis courts.

Two hundred years is a long life for a beech, a species that rarely reaches the ages of oak or yew. In late autumn it is the tree that turns this corner of the gardens copper.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 30 metres, with a trunk 4.5 metres round, the huge beech of Sydney Gardens. It stands on the right of the path along the top of the tennis courts, near the Sydney Road entrance.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the 30-metre crown turns copper

name: The Yellow Bean Tree of Sydney Gardens

location.address: On the lawn in front of the Temple of Minerva, Sydney Gardens, Bath

story:
According to the Sydney Gardens tree trail, no yellow bean tree in Britain or Ireland grows taller than this one. The trail calls it a Champion Tree, recorded on the Tree Register of the British Isles as the tallest of its kind, at 21 metres with a trunk 2.75 metres round. We have the claim from the trail rather than from the register itself, so read it as the gardens' own record.

Catalpa ovata comes from China, where its wood has a second life. The trail notes that it is the timber used for the soundboard of the guqin, the Chinese zither. In Bath the tree does a quieter job. It frames the Temple of Minerva, a replica temple moved into the gardens in 1911, standing on the lawn directly in front of it on the main promenade.

For most of the year it is simply a broad-leaved tree on a lawn. In July and August it changes character, covering itself in upright sprays of creamy white trumpet flowers, and afterwards hangs with the long thin pods that gave it its English name.

Nobody has published a planting date, so its age is an open question. If you know when the gardens' catalpa went in, tell us. Across the promenade stands a coast redwood with a thicker trunk, 2.95 metres round. The catalpa is still the taller of the two, by two metres.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the creamy white trumpet flowers in July and August and the long bean pods after. It stands directly in front of the Temple of Minerva on the main promenade, across from a coast redwood.

best_time.label: July and August, when it is covered in upright sprays of creamy white trumpet flowers

name: The Giant Sequoia of Sydney Gardens

location.address: Beside the Great Western railway line, Sydney Gardens, Bath

story:
This sequoia is thought to have arrived with the railway. When the Great Western Railway was cut through Sydney Gardens, work starting in 1839, the slopes either side of the line had to be landscaped again, and the gardens' tree trail thinks this sequoia went in as part of that replanting. On that reading it is over 170 years old. The trail is reasoning from history rather than a planting record, so take the age as its estimate.

It has done well out of the deal. The tree now stands 28 metres tall with a trunk 4.98 metres round, and it does not stand alone. It is the middle one of three big conifers along the railway fence, stops 10, 11 and 12 on the trail. First comes a blue Atlas cedar, 24 metres tall, then the sequoia, then a cedar of Lebanon that reaches 29 metres on several trunks and spreads in flat horizontal layers. Three continents' worth of conifer, lined up beside the main line from London.

To reach them, cross the bridge over the railway and take the path that leads down towards the tracks. Trains still run past it, on the same line whose cutting, if the trail is right, made room for it.

The bark is the giveaway. Giant sequoia bark is thick, red-brown and spongy, and on a trunk nearly five metres round there is a great deal of it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the thick, spongy red bark, the middle of three big conifers along the railway fence, between a blue Atlas cedar and a many-trunked cedar of Lebanon. It stands below the bridge over the line.
